opus-5.5.text:
I think the two are deeply intertwined, and if you look at the evolutionary story, you can't really separate them.

Start with the hand. When our ancestors became bipedal, the hands were freed from locomotion. That's a huge deal. Suddenly you have this incredibly dexterous end-effector, opposable thumb, fine motor control, and you can start making tools, carrying things, manipulating the world in a very rich way. And manipulation is a fantastic teacher. Every time you grasp something, you get feedback about its weight, its texture, its friction, whether it breaks or deforms. You learn physics, causality, planning, all through the hand. There's a reason people say the hand is the "outer brain." A large fraction of our motor cortex is devoted to the hands, and that's not an accident.

Then language comes in, and I'd argue it's built partly on top of that manual foundation. There are theories that gesture preceded speech, and the brain regions involved in sequencing hand actions overlap with those involved in sequencing words, Broca's area being the classic example. Tool-making is itself a kind of grammar: you have to do step A, then B, then C, with hierarchical sub-goals. So the structure of action may have scaffolded the structure of language.

But once language arrived, it did something manipulation alone could never do: it let knowledge be compressed, abstracted, and transmitted across individuals and generations. One person discovers how to make fire, and with language that discovery doesn't die with them. That's cultural accumulation, and it's what really made human intelligence explode.

So in my view, the hand gives intelligence its grounding: contact with the physical world, embodiment, real understanding of how things behave. Language gives it its reach: abstraction, communication, reasoning about things that aren't in front of you.

And this is exactly why I find the current moment in AI so interesting. Large language models have essentially taken the language half and scaled it enormously. They've absorbed humanity's compressed knowledge. But they lack the hand: they've never touched anything. For embodied intelligence, for robotics, which is what I work on, the question is how to bring those two back together: to give machines both the grounding that comes from physical interaction and the abstraction that comes from language. I don't think you get truly general intelligence with only one of them. Humans didn't.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I've thought about for a long time, partly because of what I work on. My short answer is that hands and language are two sides of the same story, and I don't think you get human-level intelligence from either one alone.

Start with the hands. When we look at the evolutionary record, the enlargement of the human brain tracks very closely with tool use. Stone tools appear long before anything we'd recognize as language. And the thing about making a tool is that it forces you to think about the future. You chip a stone not because you need it now, but because tomorrow you might need to cut something. That is planning, that is abstraction, that is a model of the world and of your own future state. The hand is really the first interface between the brain and the physical world, and the feedback from that interface is incredibly dense. Every time you grasp something, you learn about weight, friction, fragility, geometry. The brain is being trained on this constant stream of corrections.

I always say that the hand is not just an output device. It's a sensor and an actuator in one package. When a child learns to stack blocks, they're not learning stacking. They're learning physics, intuitively, through failure. That's why I'm skeptical of the idea that you can build general intelligence purely from text. The text is a compressed summary of experiences that someone had with their body.

Then language comes in, and language does something the hands can't do. It lets the lessons of one person's hands transfer to another person who never touched the object. A craftsman's thirty years of hand knowledge can be partly compressed into instructions and passed on. Language turned intelligence from an individual phenomenon into a collective one. That's the real jump. Before language, every generation had to rediscover things. After language, knowledge accumulates.

But I'd push back on one common view, which is that language is the thing that made us smart. I'd say language is the thing that made us smart together. The individual intelligence, the ability to model the world and act in it, that came from embodiment, from the loop between hand, eye and brain. Language rides on top of that. You can see it in how we talk. Almost all abstract vocabulary is borrowed from physical action. We "grasp" an idea, we "hold" a position, we "push" an argument. The metaphors give away where the thinking originally came from.

So in my work on robots, I see these as two problems that have to be solved together. We now have systems that are very good with language and very weak with hands. That's an inverted version of human development, and it produces a strange kind of intelligence. It can describe how to tie a knot perfectly and can't tie one. I think the next real breakthrough is closing that gap, giving the language side a body to be corrected by. Once you have that loop, I think you'll see learning that looks much more like what a child does, and much less like memorization.

astra-6.text:
I think manual activity and language are two deeply connected foundations of human intelligence. Working with our hands lets us intervene in the world: we grasp something, change it, observe the result, and adjust. That cycle helps us learn cause and effect, develop practical skills, and plan actions. Making a tool, for example, requires us to connect what we do now with something we want to accomplish later.

Language allows us to share and organize that experience. We can explain how a tool works, coordinate a task, or pass a discovery to someone who never witnessed it. We can also talk about things that are absent, possible, or imagined. That greatly expands the scope of thought and lets knowledge accumulate across generations.

So I would emphasize their interaction. Practical activity gives us problems to solve and experiences to communicate; language helps us reflect on those experiences and undertake more complex activities together. Human intelligence develops through that continuing exchange between action, thought, and social cooperation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think manual activity and language developed together, each expanding what the other made possible. When you make something with your hands, you have to coordinate perception and movement, anticipate a result, and adjust when the material doesn’t behave as expected. That creates a practical form of intelligence: you learn about the world by acting on it.

Language allows that experience to become shared knowledge. You can explain a technique, discuss a mistake, or plan something with another person before either of you acts. Knowledge can then accumulate across people and generations, instead of each person having to discover everything independently.

So I wouldn’t draw a sharp line between thinking with our hands and thinking with words. Manual activity gives thought concrete problems and feedback; language helps us organize, communicate, and extend what we learn. Their interaction is central to how human intelligence develops.
